instruction: How do I download Form 26AS from the Income Tax Portal?
response: Log in to the Income Tax Portal at https://www.incometax.gov.in, go to e-File > Income Tax Returns > View Form 26AS, accept the disclaimer, and continue to the TRACES/TDS-CPC page. Then click View Tax Credit (Form 26AS), choose the assessment year and view type, and download it; if you open it in HTML, you can also export it as PDF. Check Form 26AS before filing so your TDS/TCS credits match your return and you do not miss reporting taxable income that can trigger adjustments later. [page:1][page:2]

instruction: Where can I download AIS and TIS for ITR filing?
response: Log in to the Income Tax Portal and open Annual Information Statement (AIS) from the dashboard, or go through e-File > Income Tax Return > View AIS. Click Proceed to enter the AIS portal, then open the AIS tile for detailed information and the TIS tile for the category-wise summary used for prefill support; AIS can be downloaded in PDF, JSON, and CSV formats. Even after checking AIS/TIS, disclose all income sources such as savings bank interest and dividends because the department says AIS may not show every transaction and the taxpayer must report complete and accurate income in the ITR. [page:2]

instruction: Explain the difference between Form 26AS, AIS, and TIS in simple compliance terms.
response: Form 26AS now mainly shows TDS/TCS-related tax credit data on TRACES, while AIS gives a broader view of information available with the department, including tax payments, SFT data, refunds, and other reported items. TIS is the category-wise summarized version inside AIS, showing processed and accepted values for items like salary, interest, and dividend that may be used for pre-filling the return. Use all three as cross-check tools, not as substitutes for disclosure, because you still have to report complete income correctly in your ITR. [page:2][page:1]

instruction: What should I do first if I receive an income tax notice under Section 143(1)?
response: First, read the intimation carefully and identify whether it shows no demand, refund, or tax demand after processing. Compare the notice with your filed ITR, Form 26AS, AIS/TIS, TDS entries, challans, and income schedules to find the exact mismatch before taking action on the Income Tax Portal. This step matters because many Section 143(1) issues arise from omitted income, incorrect challan reporting, or mismatch in TDS details. [web:10][web:22][web:25]

instruction: How do I respond to a Section 143(1) intimation if the demand seems correct?
response: If the adjustment in the Section 143(1) intimation is correct, compute the demand, pay the tax if required, and keep proof of payment and the intimation for your records. Make sure future returns fully include income such as savings account interest, fixed deposit interest, and dividends so the same mismatch does not repeat. Processing notices often arise when return data does not align with the information available to the department. [web:10][web:22][page:2]

instruction: What if I disagree with a notice under Section 143(1)?
response: If you disagree, identify whether the issue is a mistake apparent from record, such as wrong TDS details, challan details, or a clear mismatch in processing. In such cases, use the rectification facility on the Income Tax Portal because the department states that rectification can be filed for mistakes apparent from record in an intimation under Section 143(1). Keep supporting documents ready, including Form 26AS, AIS, challans, and employer or bank certificates. [web:25][web:28]

instruction: When should I file a rectification request after a Section 143(1) intimation?
response: File a rectification request when the CPC intimation contains an obvious error on record, such as incorrect TDS/TCS data, tax payment details not considered, or another processing mismatch that can be corrected without changing the basic nature of the return. The portal FAQ says rectification can be submitted for a mistake apparent from record in an intimation under Section 143(1), but CPC rectification is generally not allowed after four years from the end of the financial year in which the intimation was passed. Act early and preserve the intimation number, supporting statements, and portal acknowledgements. [web:25][web:28]

instruction: What documents should I check before replying to a Section 143(1) notice?
response: Check your filed ITR copy, the Section 143(1) intimation, Form 26AS, AIS, TIS, salary documents, bank interest certificates, dividend statements, and tax payment challans. This review helps confirm whether you missed income, entered a wrong challan in Schedule IT, or claimed TDS that does not appear correctly in tax records. A mismatch between return data and department records is a common reason for adjustment during processing. [web:22][web:25][page:2]

instruction: What is the due date for filing ITR-1 and ITR-2 for non-audit taxpayers?
response: For FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), the due date shown in current tax filing guidance for non-audit taxpayers filing ITR-1 and ITR-2 is 31 July 2026. For most individual taxpayers choosing between ITR-1 and ITR-2, the deadline is therefore the same, but the form selection depends on the nature of income and eligibility. Filing after the due date can lead to late-filing fee consequences under Section 234F. [web:11][web:16]

instruction: Explain the practical difference between ITR-1 and ITR-2 deadlines.
response: From a deadline perspective, current guidance shows no difference for ordinary non-audit individual taxpayers: both ITR-1 and ITR-2 are due by 31 July 2026 for FY 2025-26. The real compliance difference is not the date but selecting the correct form and ensuring every taxable income item is disclosed correctly, especially interest and dividends that are often skipped in simple returns. Missing income can trigger later processing mismatches or demands even if the return was filed on time. [web:11][page:2][web:10]

instruction: Why must taxpayers disclose savings bank interest even if the amount is small?
response: Savings bank interest is still income and should be reported in the return even if tax was not deducted at source. AIS/TIS can contain interest information, and the department explicitly says taxpayers must check all related information and report complete and accurate income in the ITR because AIS may not contain everything. Not reporting small income heads repeatedly can lead to mismatch-based processing adjustments, notices, interest, and avoidable compliance friction. [page:2]

instruction: Why should dividend income be reported separately in the return?
response: Dividend income should be disclosed because it is a taxable income source and may appear in AIS/TIS under information categories used for prefill and compliance review. Taxpayers should not assume that prefilled data is complete or automatically correct; the department says complete and accurate reporting remains the taxpayer's responsibility. Omitting dividend income can contribute to a Section 143(1) mismatch if the department has corresponding third-party information. [page:2][web:10]

instruction: Can I rely only on prefilled data from the Income Tax Portal?
response: No. The Income Tax Department's AIS FAQ clearly states that AIS includes information presently available with the department and that there may be other transactions not displayed, so taxpayers are expected to report complete and accurate information in the ITR. Treat portal-prefilled data as a starting point, then reconcile it with bank statements, broker statements, salary records, and other income proofs before filing. [page:2]

instruction: What is the safest workflow before filing an ITR on the Income Tax Portal?
response: First download or review Form 26AS, AIS, and TIS from the Income Tax Portal, then compare them with your salary records, bank interest, dividend statements, capital market statements, and challans. After that, choose the correct return form, verify all income heads, confirm TDS and self-assessment tax entries, and only then submit and e-verify the return. This workflow reduces the chance of Section 143(1) adjustments caused by omitted income or mismatched tax credits. [page:1][page:2][web:10]

instruction: What are the consequences of filing ITR late?
response: Late filing can attract a fee under Section 234F, and the Income Tax Portal FAQ states that delayed filing is subject to such a fee, with a lower amount where total income is within the specified threshold. Apart from the fee, late filing increases the chance of rushed errors, delayed refunds, and unresolved mismatches in tax credits or income disclosure. Filing on time and reconciling AIS, TIS, and Form 26AS beforehand is the cleaner compliance approach. [web:16][page:1][page:2]

instruction: How should an AI assistant explain Section 234F to a taxpayer?
response: Explain that Section 234F is the late-filing fee provision that can apply when an income tax return is filed after the due date. The current Income Tax Portal FAQ states that delayed filing attracts a fee under Section 234F, and taxpayers should verify the applicable amount based on the portal's rules for the relevant year and income level. The key compliance message is simple: file by the due date and do not postpone basic paperwork. [web:16]

instruction: What common technical mistakes lead to Section 143(1) demands?
response: Common issues include not entering challan details properly, claiming incorrect TDS/TCS, omitting interest or dividend income, and filing a return that does not match information available to the department. The portal's campaigns and FAQs show that processing demand can arise when challan details are not entered in Schedule IT, and rectification is available when there is a mistake apparent from record. A careful reconciliation of portal data with personal records before filing prevents many of these routine demands. [web:22][web:25]

instruction: How should a taxpayer use AIS feedback features?
response: AIS allows taxpayers to submit feedback on information shown under TDS/TCS, SFT, and other information categories, and the portal says the modified value becomes visible after feedback is submitted. Use this feature when a transaction is duplicated, belongs to another person, is partially correct, or otherwise needs correction, but still ensure the final ITR reports complete and accurate income. Feedback improves the data trail, yet it does not remove the taxpayer's responsibility to disclose all taxable income. [page:2]

instruction: What should a taxpayer remember after downloading AIS or TIS?
response: Downloading AIS or TIS is only the review step, not the filing step. After download, the taxpayer should verify whether salary, bank interest, dividends, tax payments, and other reported items align with personal records, and then disclose all taxable income correctly in the return. The department expressly notes that AIS may not contain all transactions, so full reporting is still mandatory. [page:2]

instruction: Write a compliance-focused reply for a taxpayer who says: 'My ITR was simple, so I skipped bank interest and dividends.'
response: Even in a simple return, skipping bank interest or dividend income is risky because all taxable income sources should be disclosed. AIS/TIS may contain such items, and the department states taxpayers must report complete and accurate information even if some transactions are not fully reflected there; omissions can lead to Section 143(1) adjustments, extra tax demand, and late correction work on the Income Tax Portal. The boring paperwork matters because small omissions often create disproportionate compliance trouble later. [page:2][web:10]
